## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Fundamentals of Security and Robustness for AI
  Code                    M2 · P2 (brochure) — official code not published (course description not published)
  Team and workload       Instructor: master's team · \~24 h · the mathematical foundation of learning security: threat model, adversarial examples (FGSM/PGD proven), adversarial training and its cost, certification (randomized smoothing), trojans, poisoning, extraction and membership inference, up to evaluation protocols (RobustBench) and defensive deployment.
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2}[Outside the recommended track]{.badge .position} · M2 program being finalized
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer shipping a model who must anticipate attacks. **Empirical first**: clean accuracy 94% → 11% under PGD ε=8/255; an ad-hoc defense that dies under an adaptive attack — then we name threat model, adversarial training, certification.

Adversarial examples, poisoning, extraction, RobustBench — defensive foundations.

### What you will be able to do

-   Write the threat model of a system: what the adversary knows, can modify, and seeks to obtain;
-   Build adversarial examples by optimization (FGSM, PGD, CW) and understand what AutoAttack guarantees;
-   Measure the adversarial phenomenon with the right distances and separate the problem from plain classification errors;
-   Train a robust model (adversarial training) and quantify its extra cost in compute and accuracy;
-   Certify robustness by randomized smoothing or formal verification, and state what the certificate covers;
-   Detect and analyze trojans, backdoors and data poisoning;
-   Situate intellectual-property attacks: model stealing, membership inference;
-   Transpose the approach to LLMs and graphs, and read a robustness benchmark (RobustBench) with a critical eye.

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module offered in period 2, outside the recommended track: it is the "security" foundation on which the specialized modules at the end of the master open. **Prerequisites**: [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) (gradient training, convolutions — the optimization attacks are grafted onto it); [Advanced Graph Neural Networks](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html), whose Nettack attack from ch. 7 is one of the starting points of the "graphs" chapter; and the federated learning part of [Emerging ML](../m1p1-emerging-ml/index.html), where Byzantine servers prepare the poisoning question.

**Downstream modules**: [Explainability, Security, Privacy of LLMs](../m2-explainability-security-privacy-llms/index.html) directly takes up this taxonomy to deploy it on LLMs (jailbreaks, injections, defenses in depth, ch. 5–6); the threat-model reflexes also serve the operational guardrails of the [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) module.

### Course outline

-   **Recap: the foundation and the vocabulary** — attacker, surface, guarantee: the lexicon without which nothing can be discussed.
-   **Threat model and taxonomy of attacks** — classify attacks by knowledge (white/black/gray box) and by goal.
-   **Adversarial examples: the phenomenon and its distances** — the experimental phenomenon, and why the choice of distance changes everything.
-   **Optimization-based attacks: FGSM, PGD, CW, AutoAttack** — the derived and proven attacks, up to standardized evaluation.
-   **Defenses: adversarial training** — the reference defense, its minimax formulation and its real cost.
-   **Certification: randomized smoothing and formal verification** — going from "it resists tests" to "it is proven", and under what conditions.
-   **Trojans and backdoors** — models that behave well until the attacker's chosen trigger.
-   **Data poisoning** — corrupting learning upstream, when only the data is touched.
-   **Model stealing and membership inference** — the intellectual-property and confidentiality attacks, a bridge to the LLM privacy module.
-   **Beyond images: LLMs and graphs** — adversarial prompts, structure attacks: the foundation transported to the master's objects.
-   **Evaluating and deploying** — rigorous protocols (RobustBench) and defensive deployment decisions.
-   **Exercises / Labs** — implement FGSM/PGD, adversarial training and a graph attack.
-   **References** — the founding papers of each family of attacks and defenses.

### How to study this module

-   Attack before defending: implement PGD from the very first week — one understands a defense only after failing to break it.
-   For each attack, write formally what the adversary optimizes, under which constraints, with what knowledge: this is the central discipline of the module.
-   Beware of "miracle defenses": train yourself to identify why a defense not evaluated against an adaptive attack proves nothing.
-   Redo the numbers of the cost of robustness (accuracy, training time) on a small model: the trade-off is better seen than read.
-   Reread ch. 7 of Advanced GNN and the Byzantine part of Emerging ML at the start of the module: the graphs and poisoning chapters build directly on them.

::: note
[The LLGA perspective]{.tag} Robustness is a crossroads of the master: adversarial examples are born on images, and carry over to graphs (structure attacked around a node) and to LLMs (hostile prompts) — the three families of models of the LLGA. Completed by differential privacy and by the dedicated LLM module, this foundation makes you able to audit a learning system, a skill that European regulation now expects from industry as much as from research laboratories.
:::

## 0. Recap: the foundation and the vocabulary {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Prerequisites (M1/M2 modules)
:::

-   **Networks and optimization** (cf. Deep Learning module): stochastic gradient descent, backpropagation, softmax and the cross-entropy loss $\ell(f(x), y) = -\log p_f(y \mid x)$, convolutions — the playing field for all the attacks of ch. 2-5;
-   **Generalization** (cf. Machine Learning module ch. 7): empirical risk vs true risk, overfitting — the vocabulary to understand why robustness *generalizes poorly* (ch. 4);
-   **Statistics** (Refresher Statistics): hypothesis testing, type I/II errors, the Neyman-Pearson lemma — the hidden tool behind randomized smoothing (ch. 5) and membership inference (ch. 8);
-   **Differential privacy** (cf. Emerging ML module ch. 5): the $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ definition, Gaussian mechanism, composition — reused without re-proving in ch. 7-8;
-   **Byzantine robustness and federated learning** (cf. Emerging ML module ch. 4): malicious clients, robust aggregation — ch. 7 is its "centralized data" counterpart;
-   **LLM security** (cf. Explainability, Security and Privacy of LLMs module): jailbreaks, injections, extraction — ch. 9 systematically refers to that module.
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Robustness, security, safety]{.tag} Three properties that are often confused: **robustness** is a mathematical property of the model (bounding the variation of the output under a constraint on the input); **security** is a property of the *system* faced with an intentional attacker (it requires a threat model); **safety** covers even unintentional harm (bias, in-distribution errors). This module covers the first two; the third crosses over with the Responsible AI and Explainability modules. A model can be robust and not safe, and vice versa.
:::

::: note
[Module method]{.tag} Each chapter follows the same grid: (i) formalize the attack as an optimization problem; (ii) prove what is provable (FGSM in ch. 3, the hidden regularization of adversarial training in ch. 4, the certified radius in ch. 5); (iii) give the standard defense *and the way it breaks* — a defense not evaluated by adaptive attack is not a defense. Labs on MNIST/CIFAR (FGSM, PGD, adversarial training) then full audits.
:::

## 1. Threat model and taxonomy of attacks {#ch1}

Concrete scene: a fraud detector survives FGSM and falls under iterated PGD. This chapter sets the threat model before patches.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Evaluating only weak attacks; obfuscated defenses (security through obscurity); ignoring poisoning / model extraction.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Threat model]{.tag} Every security analysis starts with three explicit assumptions: the attacker's **capabilities** — *white-box* (architecture and weights known), *gray-box* (architecture known, weights not), *black-box* (access only to the predictions, possibly limited in queries or without scores); the **timing** of the attack — at training time (poisoning, backdoor) or at inference time (evasion, extraction, membership inference); the **goal** — untargeted error, targeted error (one specific class), information leakage, theft of intellectual property, denial of service. Changing one assumption changes the whole analysis: most misunderstandings in the field come from different implicit threat models.
:::

  Attack                          Timing      Access required            Goal                                         Chapter
  ------------------------------- ----------- -------------------------- -------------------------------------------- ---------
  Evasion (adversarial example)   inference   white → black (transfer)   error, targeted or not                       2-3
  Poisoning                       training    write access to the data   degrade / bias                               7
  Backdoor (trojan)               training    data + trigger             hidden rule triggered                        6
  Extraction (model stealing)     inference   black, score API           copy the model                               8
  Membership inference            inference   black, score API           "was this individual in the training set?"   8

::: note
[Reference framework]{.tag} This taxonomy (evasion / poisoning / extraction / inference) is the one from the survey by Biggio & Roli (*Wild Patterns: Ten Years After the Rise of Adversarial Machine Learning*, 2018), which also structures the evaluation frameworks (ch. 10). The important conceptual point: unlike classical software security (hunting for bugs), here the *attack surface is the prediction function itself* — every non-trivial classifier has decision boundaries, and boundaries have two sides.
:::

## 2. Adversarial examples: the phenomenon and its distances {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Adversarial example (Szegedy et al., 2014)]{.tag} For a classifier $f : \mathcal{X} \to \{1, \dots, K\}$, an adversarial example of $x$ (of class $y$) is an $\tilde{x} = x + \delta$ such that $f(\tilde{x}) \neq f(x) = y$ (or a target class $t$ chosen by the attacker: $f(\tilde{x}) = t$) while $\\|\delta\\|$ is "small" in the sense of a distance to be fixed. Szegedy et al. showed that these points exist at surprising density around *every* test point, for networks with very high accuracy — they are not isolated misclassified points, but imperceptible perturbations of correctly classified points.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — The three useful balls]{.tag} $$ \\|\delta\\|_0 = \|\{j : \delta_j \neq 0\}\| \quad (\text{modified pixels}), \qquad \\|\delta\\|_2 = \Big(\sum_j \delta_j^2\Big)^{1/2} \quad (\text{energy}), \qquad \\|\delta\\|_\infty = \max_j \|\delta_j\| \quad (\text{max amplitude}). $$ The associated balls $B_p(x, \varepsilon)$ define the attacker's **budget**. Standard protocols: $\varepsilon = 0.3$ in $L_\infty$ on MNIST (pixels in $[0,1]$), $\varepsilon = 8/255$ on CIFAR-10 (ch. 10). Each norm models a different threat: sporadically altered sensors ($L_0$), physical noise ($L_2$), brightness/contrast ($L_\infty$).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — The linear hypothesis (Goodfellow et al., 2015)]{.tag} Even a *linear* classifier admits adversarial examples in high dimension. For $f(x) = w^\top x + b$ (the score of one class), and $\\|\delta\\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon$: $$ \|f(x + \delta) - f(x)\| = \|w^\top \delta\| \leq \varepsilon\, \\|w\\|_1. $$ In dimension $d$ with typical weights $\|w_j\| \approx m$, the shift reaches $\varepsilon\, m\, d$: each coordinate only "moves" by $\varepsilon$, but the $d$ contributions *add up*. With $d \sim 10^5$ pixels, a relative perturbation of $1\%$ per coordinate suffices to change the score by several logistic units.

::: proof
Upper bound: Hölder's inequality $ \|w^\top \delta\| \leq \\|w\\|_1 \\|\delta\\|_\infty$, attained for $\delta = \varepsilon\, \mathrm{sign}(w)$. The order of magnitude follows by taking $\\|w\\|_1 \approx m d$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Transfer and the physical world]{.tag} Two properties make the threat practical: (i) **transfer** — an adversarial example computed on one (substitute) model often fools another model, including one with a different architecture: the black-box attack reduces to the white-box case; (ii) the **physical world** — Kurakin et al. (2017) printed adversarial images: the perturbation survives printing, photography and change of viewpoint. Adversarial examples on tabular data also exist (transaction amounts adjusted below the thresholds of detection rules); note that on GBDTs, since the function is piecewise constant, gradient-based attacks do not apply directly — one then attacks by discrete search or via a differentiable substitute.
:::

## 3. Optimization-based attacks: FGSM, PGD, CW, AutoAttack {#ch3}

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — The evasion problem]{.tag} Untargeted attack with budget $\varepsilon$ (norm $p$): $$ \max_{\delta}\ \ell(f_\theta(x + \delta),\, y) \quad \text{subject to}\quad \\|\delta\\|_p \leq \varepsilon,\ x + \delta \in [0,1]^d, $$ where $\ell$ is the cross-entropy. Targeted version: maximize $\ell(f(x+\delta), y) - \ell(f(x+\delta), t)$ (push the target class $t$ up *and* the true one down). The whole difficulty is the non-concave *inner* max — it cannot be evaluated exactly, only lower-bounded (attacks) or overestimated.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — FGSM = linearization of the problem (Goodfellow et al., 2015)]{.tag} To first order in $\delta$, $\ell(x + \delta) \approx \ell(x) + \nabla_x \ell(x)^\top \delta$. The maximum of this linear approximation over the $L_\infty$ ball is attained at $$ \delta^\star = \varepsilon\, \mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_x \ell(x)\big) \qquad (\text{Fast Gradient Sign Method}), $$ with increase $\varepsilon\, \\|\nabla_x \ell(x)\\|_1$. Over the $L_2$ ball: $\delta^\star = \varepsilon\, \nabla_x \ell(x) / \\|\nabla_x \ell(x)\\|_2$ (FGM).

::: proof
Hölder: for every $\delta$ with $\\|\delta\\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon$, $g^\top \delta \leq \sum_j \|g_j\|\,\|\delta_j\| \leq \varepsilon \sum_j \|g_j\| = \varepsilon \\|g\\|_1$, with $g = \nabla_x \ell(x)$. There is equality iff $\|\delta_j\| = \varepsilon$ and $\mathrm{sign}(\delta_j) = \mathrm{sign}(g_j)$ for every nonzero $j$ — which is exactly $\delta^\star$. For $L_2$: Cauchy-Schwarz $g^\top\delta \leq \\|g\\|_2\\|\delta\\|_2 \leq \varepsilon\\|g\\|_2$, equality iff $\delta$ is collinear with $g$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — PGD (Madry et al., 2018)]{.tag} The linearization is only valid locally; one iterates while re-projecting onto the ball and onto $[0,1]^d$ (projection $=$ clamping $\min(\max(x+\delta - \varepsilon, x - \varepsilon), x + \varepsilon)$ for $L_\infty$): $$ \delta^{(k+1)} = \Pi_{B_\infty(\varepsilon)}\Big(\delta^{(k)} + \alpha\, \mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_x \ell(x + \delta^{(k)})\big)\Big), \qquad \delta^{(0)} \in \{\,0,\ \text{or uniform in } B_\infty(\varepsilon)\,\}, $$ with step size $\alpha \approx 2.5\,\varepsilon/K$ for $K$ iterations, and multiple restarts (the inner objective is non-concave: several starting points are sampled). PGD is the qualitative standard: "robust to PGD" has become a (too convenient) synonym for robust.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — CW (Carlini & Wagner, 2017)]{.tag} Attack optimized on the *logit margin* $Z(x)$, with the change of variable $\delta = \tfrac{1}{2}(\tanh(w) + 1) - x$ to get rid of the box constraints: $$ \min_{w}\ \Big\\| \tfrac{1}{2}(\tanh(w)+1) - x \Big\\|_2^2 + c \cdot \max\big(Z(x+\delta)_y - \max_{t \neq y} Z(x+\delta)_t,\ -\kappa\big), $$ with a bisection search over $c$ and confidence $\kappa \geq 0$. CW-L2 long remained the most effective attack — and the tool that demolished the first generation of defenses (ch. 4).
:::

::: note
[Black box and standard evaluation]{.tag} Without gradients: (i) *transfer* (ch. 2); (ii) *score-based* attacks (gradient estimation by queries, random square attacks); (iii) *decision-based* attacks (random walk on the boundary). For evaluation, one no longer uses a single isolated attack but **AutoAttack** (Croce & Hein, 2020): a parameter-free ensemble — APGD-CE, APGD-T, FAB-T, Square — which cuts the displayed "robustness" of several defended models by more than 10 points. Rule of the module: *any robustness measure is worth exactly the worst attack that has been tried*.
:::

```python
# FGSM and PGD in about ten lines (PyTorch)
def fgsm(model, x, y, eps):
    x.requires_grad_(True)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    return (x + eps * x.grad.sign()).clamp(0, 1).detach()

def pgd(model, x, y, eps, alpha, iters, restarts=1):
    worst, worst_loss = None, float("-inf")
    for _ in range(restarts):
        d = torch.zeros_like(x).uniform_(-eps, eps)      # random start
        for _ in range(iters):
            d.requires_grad_(True)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(model((x + d).clamp(0, 1)), y)
            g = torch.autograd.grad(loss, d)[0]          # gradient of the inner max
            with torch.no_grad():
                d = (d + alpha * g.sign()).clamp(-eps, eps)
        x_adv = (x + d).clamp(0, 1).detach()
        l = F.cross_entropy(model(x_adv), y).item()      # candidate loss
        if l > worst_loss:                               # keep the worst case
            worst, worst_loss = x_adv, l
    return worst
```

## 4. Defenses: adversarial training {#ch4}

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Adversarial training (Madry et al., 2018)]{.tag} One minimizes the *robust* risk, a min-max problem: $$ \min_{\theta}\ \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}\Big[\ \max_{\\|\delta\\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon} \ell\big(f_\theta(x + \delta),\, y\big)\ \Big], $$ the inner max being approximated by PGD (def. 3.3): at each descent step, each example is *replaced* by its current adversarial version. This is a form of stochastic minimax; in practice: training cost multiplied by the number of PGD iterations (typically 7-10).
:::

```python
# full lab: PGD-AT on MNIST (the min-max, line by line)
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F

model = nn.Sequential(                                 # small CNN
    nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
    nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
    nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 10))

def pgd(model, x, y, eps, steps, alpha):               # the inner MAX (def. 3.3)
    d = torch.zeros_like(x).uniform_(-eps, eps)        # random start
    for _ in range(steps):
        d.requires_grad_(True)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model((x + d).clamp(0, 1)), y)
        g = torch.autograd.grad(loss, d)[0].sign()
        with torch.no_grad():
            d = (d + alpha * g).clamp(-eps, eps)
    return (x + d).clamp(0, 1).detach()

opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
eps, steps, alpha = 0.3, 7, 0.3 * 2.5 / 7             # Madry protocol
for epoch in range(10):
    for x, y in train_loader:
        x_adv = pgd(model, x, y, eps, steps, alpha)    # approximate the max...
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x_adv), y)        # ...then minimize (outer MIN)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

def accuracy(model, x, y, attack=None):                # honest evaluation
    xb = x if attack is None else attack(model, x, y)
    return (model(xb).argmax(1) == y).float().mean().item()

# mandatory final report: BOTH numbers (def. 10.1)
print("standard :", accuracy(model, x_test, y_test))
print("robuste  :", accuracy(model, x_test, y_test,
      lambda m, x, y: pgd(m, x, y, eps, 50, 0.01)))    # strong PGD in evaluation
```

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — The min-max, proven on a linear case]{.tag} For a linear classifier $f(x) = w^\top x + b$ and the hinge loss $\ell(y\, f(x)) = \max(0,\ 1 - y\, f(x))$ (labels $y \in \{\pm1\}$), the $L_\infty$ robust risk reads $$ \max_{\\|\delta\\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon}\ \max\big(0,\ 1 - y\,(w^\top(x+\delta) + b)\big) \;=\; \max\big(0,\ 1 - y\,(w^\top x + b) + \varepsilon \\|w\\|_1\big). $$ Adversarial training of a linear model with hinge loss is therefore *exactly* an $L_1$-regularized SVM regression with coefficient $\varepsilon$: robustness acts as a penalty on the weights.

::: proof
The max of $1 - y\,(w^\top x + b) - y\, w^\top \delta$ over the ball is attained (Hölder, cf. proof of thm. 3.2) at $\delta^\star = -\varepsilon\, y\, \mathrm{sign}(w)$, and equals $1 - y(w^\top x + b) + \varepsilon \\|w\\|_1$. If this quantity is negative, the robust hinge loss equals $0$ — hence the global $\max(0, \cdot)$: the outer and inner max commute because the hinge is increasing. Summing over the examples gives $\sum_i \max(0, 1 - y_i f(x_i) + \varepsilon\\|w\\|_1)$: the term $\varepsilon \\|w\\|_1$ does not depend on $i$, it is the $L_1$ penalty. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[What Theorem 4.2 teaches]{.tag} (i) robustness has a *statistical price*: penalizing $w$ reduces the effective margin, hence the standard accuracy — the robustness/accuracy trade-off is not a bug; (ii) the scale of $w$ is the real lever: hence in practice bounded weights, input normalization, shared weights (cf. Deep Learning modules, regularization chapter). Schmidt et al. (2019) formalize point (i): robust generalization requires *more data* than standard generalization.
:::

::: thm
[Decomposition of the robust error (TRADES, Zhang et al., 2019)]{.tag} For every classifier, the robust error (worst case within the balls) decomposes as $$ \mathcal{R}_{rob} \;\leq\; \mathcal{R}_{nat} \;+\; \mathcal{R}_{bdy}, $$ natural error + "boundary error" (points correctly classified but within $\varepsilon$ of a decision boundary). TRADES explicitly optimizes the second term via a KL term between $f(x)$ and $f(x+\delta)$ — and dominates pure PGD-AT on several benchmarks. "Naive" adversarial training maximizes the margin; TRADES shows that one must also *smooth* the model.
:::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Robust overfitting (Rice et al., 2020)]{.tag} A specific phenomenon: during adversarial training, *test* robustness peaks abruptly (often within the first few dozen epochs) then *decreases* while train robustness keeps rising — a robust overfitting, mitigated (not solved) by early stopping and massive data augmentation (Rebuffi et al., 2021). Counter-intuitive but systematically reproduced: it is one of the most solid experimental facts in the field.
:::

::: note
[How not to defend]{.tag} The 2017-2019 decade produced hundreds of "masked-gradient" defenses (shrinkage, discretization, derandomization...) broken as soon as they were attacked *adaptively*: Athalye et al. (2018) ("Obfuscated gradients give a false sense of security") break several of them with a backward-pass attack (backward-pass differentiable approximation) and reparameterization; Tramèr et al. (2020) codify the answer: *every defense must be evaluated by an attack that knows it*. Lab 3 enforces this protocol. For networks already deployed without retraining: detection (filters, distribution detection), rejection/abstention, preprocessing (quantization, JPEG compression, total-variation denoising — Guo et al., 2017); useful against *transferred* attacks, these "palliative" defenses are systematically bypassed by an attack that knows the filter — always test against an adapted attack.
:::

## 5. Certification: randomized smoothing and formal verification {#ch5}

Chapters 3-4 bound robustness *from below* (attacks) — no guarantee about what has not been found. Certification bounds it *from above*: a radius within which *no* perturbation of a given budget can change the prediction.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Randomized smoothing (Cohen, Rosenfeld & Kolter, 2019)]{.tag} Let $f$ be a base classifier and $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$. The **smoothed** classifier is $$ g(x) = \arg\max_{c}\ \mathbb{P}\big(f(x + \varepsilon) = c\big), $$ the most likely class when the input is perturbed with Gaussian noise. $g$ inherits a *tight* $L_2$ guarantee (see thm. 5.2), computable for any black-box $f$ — it is the only certification method that has scaled (ImageNet).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Certified radius (Cohen et al., 2019)]{.tag} Let $c_A = g(x)$, $p_A = \mathbb{P}(f(x + \varepsilon) = c_A)$ and $p_B = \max_{c \neq c_A} \mathbb{P}(f(x + \varepsilon) = c)$. If one knows bounds $\underline{p_A} \leq p_A$ and $p_B \leq \overline{p_B}$ with $\underline{p_A} \> \overline{p_B}$, then $g$ predicts $c_A$ *over the entire* $L_2$ ball of radius $$ R = \frac{\sigma}{2}\Big(\Phi^{-1}(\underline{p_A}) - \Phi^{-1}(\overline{p_B})\Big), $$ where $\Phi^{-1}$ is the inverse of the standard Gaussian cumulative distribution function.

::: proof
(Sketch — the full version is in the paper.) Separation lemma: for every Borel set $S$ and every $\delta$, if $\mathbb{P}_{\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2I)}(\varepsilon \in S) \geq p$ and $\mathbb{P}(\varepsilon \in S - \delta) \leq q$, then $\\|\delta\\|_2 \geq \tfrac{\sigma}{2}(\Phi^{-1}(p) - \Phi^{-1}(q))$. Proof of the lemma: the most powerful test for distinguishing $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2I)$ from $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\delta, \sigma^2 I)$ (Neyman-Pearson lemma) is thresholding the likelihood ratio $-\delta^\top \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2}\\|\delta\\|_2^2$ — Gaussian linear, hence $\delta^\top \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2\\|\delta\\|_2^2)$. Express the two probabilities via $\Phi$ and eliminate the threshold: this yields the crude bound $\\|\delta\\|_2 \geq \sigma\,(\Phi^{-1}(p) - \Phi^{-1}(q))$; the tight analysis of Cohen et al. then refines the constant to $\tfrac{\sigma}{2}$ (the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ comes from the optimal allocation of the budget between the two hypotheses). Application: set $S = f^{-1}(c_A)$; $p_A = \mathbb{P}(x + \varepsilon \in S)$ and every point of the ball $B_2(x, R)$ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(\cdot \in S) \> \mathbb{P}(\cdot \in S')$ for every competing class $S'$ — class $c_A$ remains the majority, so $g$ equals $c_A$ there. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — Certification in practice]{.tag} $p_A, p_B$ are unknown: they are *estimated* by Monte Carlo — $n_0$ draws to choose $g(x)$, $n$ draws to build a binomial confidence interval (exact: Clopper-Pearson) on $p_A$; $\overline{p_B}$ is taken as one minus that bound. The procedure is *sound* with probability $1 - \alpha$ — the final guarantee combines sampling randomness and a deterministic theorem. One then plots **certified accuracy** vs radius: a curve necessarily below the empirical curve (attacks), the gap measuring our ignorance. Precious link: randomized smoothing is the classification analogue of the Gaussian mechanism of DP (cf. Emerging ML module ch. 5); the "PixelDP" variant (Lecuyer et al., 2019) makes it explicit.
:::

::: note
[Deterministic certification]{.tag} For ReLU networks, local robustness is decidable: encode the network and the ball as arithmetic constraints (mixed linear/ReLU) and ask a solver — Reluplex (Katz et al., 2017) extends the simplex to ReLU constraints and has verified aircraft collision-avoidance networks. Complete but exponential: in practice one uses *incomplete* methods (interval bounds, zonotopes) that quickly certify a smaller region. Decision trees: trivial exact certification by enumerating the leaves reachable within the ball — one of the rare cases where "classical" tabular is structurally more certifiable than deep.
:::

## 6. Trojans and backdoors {#ch6}

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Backdoor / Trojan horse (Gu et al., 2017)]{.tag} A backdoored model $f$ behaves normally on clean inputs, but an $\mathcal{A}(x)$ carrying the *trigger* (patch, high-frequency pattern, watermark) is classified into the target class: $$ f(x) \approx f_{clean}(x) \ \text{on the clean distribution}, \qquad f(x + \tau) = t \ \text{almost always}. $$ Unlike evasion (ch. 2-3), the attack is *cast* into training: BadNets obtains it by contaminating a fraction of the training data (legitimate examples + trigger + target label) — validation accuracy remains excellent, which makes the contamination undetectable by standard metrics.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.2 — Clean-label (Shafahi et al., 2018)]{.tag} "Poison Frogs": the attacker controls *no labels*. One fabricates *a single* poisoned example: starting from an image of the target class $t$, it is optimized to enter into a **feature collision** with the victim image (close in the latent space of a pre-trained network) while remaining visibly of class $t$. After fine-tuning, the victim (a clean image!) is classified as $t$. A single data point suffices in transfer — the worst nightmare of collaborative data pipelines; cf. Emerging ML module ch. 4 for the federated case (malicious clients) and ch. 7 for poisoning at scale.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.3 — Detection: trigger reverse-engineering (Neural Cleanse, Wang et al., 2019)]{.tag} For each class $c$, one optimizes the *minimal* perturbation $\delta_c$ that forces all inputs toward $c$; a backdoored model exhibits an anomaly: for the target class $t$, $\\|\delta_t\\|_1$ is noticeably smaller (the existing trigger provides a "shortcut"). The anomaly is detected by median absolute deviation (MAD), the trigger is reconstructed, then one *repairs*: pruning the hyperactive neurons under the trigger, or fine-tuning/unlearning on the reconstructed inputs.
:::

::: note
[Limits and practice]{.tag} Existing defenses assume *small, fixed, patch-shaped* triggers: adaptive triggers (distributed, input-dependent, semantic — "a cap" — or sample-specific) escape reverse-engineering. The second family of detection is **spectral** (Spectral Signatures, Tran, Li & Madry, NeurIPS 2018): backdoored examples form a cluster in the space of last-layer activations — outliers are isolated in the principal directions (SVD of the activation matrix) and removed from the training set; complementary to reverse-engineering (it assumes no trigger shape), but broken by attacks that minimize their spectral signature. Deployment rules: traceable data chain, audited source models, dedicated tests ("does the model react oddly to this pattern?"), and above all monitoring the *region* around the model (ch. 10); cf. Explainability, Security and Privacy of LLMs module ch. 5 for the LLM variant (instruction poisoning).
:::

## 7. Data poisoning {#ch7}

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Poisoning]{.tag} The attacker modifies a fraction $\rho$ of the training set before learning. Variants: **label flipping** ($(x_i, y_i) \to (x_i, 1 - y_i)$; or chosen "optimal" flips), **feature manipulation** ($x_i \to x_i + \delta_i$, labels intact — covers the clean-label attack of ch. 6), and **insertion** of forged examples. Goal: global degradation, targeted bias on a subgroup, or a backdoor. The optimal attack (Biggio et al., 2012, on SVMs) maximizes the attacker's *validation* risk on the contaminated data — solved by deriving the optimality condition (gradient of the final model with respect to the poison point, via the implicit function theorem).
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Where flipping matters]{.tag} With a fixed budget of flips, the impact on the risk is maximized by moving the boundary *as close as possible* to well-classified points with a large margin: flipping a point very close to the boundary moves the classifier little (it was already almost an error); flipping points *deep* inside a class pulls the boundary toward the dense zone of the other class. Empirical consequence: a few percent of "smart" flips degrade more than many random flips — and strong regularization dampens both (the regularized classifier "resists" isolated points).
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.3 — Influence functions (Koh & Liang, 2017)]{.tag} The influence of a training point $z$ on the prediction at $x_{test}$ measures what would happen if $z$ were upweighted by an $\varepsilon \to 0$: $$ \mathcal{I}(z, x_{test}) = -\nabla_\theta \ell(x_{test};\hat\theta)^\top H_{\hat\theta}^{-1}\, \nabla_\theta \ell(z; \hat\theta), \qquad H_{\hat\theta} = \nabla_\theta^2 \hat R(\hat\theta), $$ estimable without retraining (Hessian-vector products, LiSSA). It is the "defensive" tool: poisons with strong negative influence are candidates for audit/removal — and the symmetric offensive tool: crafting poisons with maximal influence. In practice: filtering by influence, anomaly detection in the gradients, truncated losses (robust to outliers), and for the distributed setting, Byzantine aggregates (cf. Emerging ML module ch. 4: trimmed mean, coordinate-wise median...).
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.4 — Data hygiene, the real defense]{.tag} Deduplication (poisons are often amplified *duplicates*), human validation of examples with high loss + high influence, provenance (data lineage, cf. ML Ops module), and trust budgets: every external source enters with a fraction cap. DP (Emerging ML module ch. 5) bounds *by construction* the effect of an individual point — an $\varepsilon$-DP robust to poisoning at the price of utility: the trade-off is the same as in ch. 8 for privacy.
:::

## 8. Model stealing and membership inference {#ch8}

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Extraction / model stealing]{.tag} The attacker queries a prediction API to *reconstruct* the model (or a functional equivalent). Two regimes (Jagielski et al., 2020): high **accuracy** (a copy that predicts well on the task — functional counterfeiting) or high **fidelity** (a copy that imitates the boundary, *including* its errors — to build transferable adversarial examples).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 8.2 — Exact extraction of a logistic regression (Tramèr et al., 2016)]{.tag} If the API exposes $p(y=1 \mid x) = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$, then $d + 1$ queries on linearly independent $x$'s suffice to recover $(w, b)$ *exactly*.

::: proof
From $p = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$, one gets $\mathrm{logit}(p) = \log \frac{p}{1-p} = w^\top x + b$ (the API gives $p$, the logit is a function of $p$). Each query therefore provides a *linear* equation in $(w, b)$; with $d+1$ independent points (with affine coordinate 1), the linear system has a unique solution. If the API rounds the probabilities, each equation becomes a bounding interval — one solves by linear programming, with a polynomial number of additional queries. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 8.3 — Membership inference (MIA, Shokri et al., 2017)]{.tag} The attacker wants to decide whether an individual $(x, y)$ was part of the training set — a *confidentiality* attack (membership itself can be sensitive: medical record, fraud). Canonical attack: train *shadow models* on similar data, label member/non-member, learn this membership classifier on the confidence scores. Modern version (Carlini et al., 2022, "LiRA"): likelihood ratio test — for each target, an *ensemble* of shadow models with/without the target estimates the two logit densities $\mathcal{N}(\mu_{in}, \sigma_{in}^2)$, $\mathcal{N}(\mu_{out}, \sigma_{out}^2)$; the optimal test is applied. Honest metric: TPR at low FPR (0.1\\%) — that is where membership is dangerous.
:::

::: note
[Defenses and links]{.tag} Reduce the exposed precision (top-1 only, rounding — partial effectiveness, cf. prop. 8.2), limit/monitor queries (model stealing is a *volume* attack), model watermarking (cf. LLMs / Explainability-Security-Privacy module ch. 9); the only strong guarantee is **training-time DP** (DP-SGD, cf. Emerging ML module ch. 5; Privacy and Uncertainty M2 module): an $(\varepsilon, \delta)$ bounds the advantage of *any* MIA — at the price of a utility loss to be budgeted. MIA is also the auditing tool for synthetic data (cf. Boosting/Foundation Tabular module ch. 8): same box, same tool, two communities.
:::

## 9. Beyond images: LLMs and graphs {#ch9}

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — LLM robustness (overview)]{.tag} Attacks move from the pixel to the *token*: jailbreaks by suffixing (concatenate a **universal adversarial suffix** optimized by gradient — GCG, Zou et al., 2023: the same mathematics as PGD, on discrete tokens), prompt injections (the payload sits in a document read by the agent), poisoning of the fine-tuning corpus or of RLHF preferences. The *Explainability, Security and Privacy of LLMs* module (M2) covers all of this in depth; we retain here only the mathematical continuity: maximize $P(\text{harmful output} \mid x + \delta)$ under *discrete* constraints — hence coordinate-wise optimizations and tree searches rather than gradient signs.
:::

::: thm
[Case study 9.2 — Graphs: Nettack (Zügner et al., 2018)]{.tag} GNNs inherit a *relational* attack surface: the attacker modifies edges, node features, or *other nodes* in the same component. Nettack perturbs the structure and features of a citation graph to change the classification of a target node, by greedy search on marginal gains — with a **direct** effect (neighborhood) and an **indirect** one (perturbations of the neighbors of neighbors modify the aggregations): the classification of a node flips with a few dozen modifications *invisible* at the scale of the graph. Non-robustness is aggravated by propagation; the dedicated defenses (certification by propagation, robust learning) are covered in ch. 7 of the *Advanced GNN* module (M2) — this chapter only lays down the prerequisites.
:::

::: note
[And tabular models?]{.tag} On GBDTs (piecewise constant), no gradient: threshold attacks (moving $x_j$ just beyond the active splits), differentiable substitutes, or discrete search dominate — and exact certification by leaf enumeration (ch. 5) is trivial there. Robustness therefore depends strongly on the model *family*: the same system can be vulnerable via its scoring network and certifiable via its GBDT — one more argument for fallback architectures (ch. 10).
:::

## 10. Evaluating and deploying {#ch10}

::: def
[Definition 10.1 — RobustBench (Croce et al., 2021)]{.tag} Standardized protocol: fixed threats per dataset ($L_\infty$, $\varepsilon = 8/255$ on CIFAR-10; $L_2$; self-supervised attacks), evaluation by **AutoAttack** + adapted attacks, public leaderboard, reproducible models and details. Reporting rules: *standard AND robust accuracy*, attack budget, number of restarts, training cost. Without these elements, a robustness number is not information.
:::

::: thm
[In-depth deployment (layered defense)]{.tag}

1.  **Reduce the surface**: do not expose full scores (ch. 8), query quotas, query monitoring (volumes, distributions);
2.  **Detect**: adversarial-example detectors, drift/OOD detection (cf. ML Ops module): rejection is an honest defense;
3.  **Resist**: adversarial training (ch. 4) or certification (ch. 5) where the risk justifies it — otherwise: a secondary "hardened" version;
4.  **Limit the damage**: fallback models (falling back to a certifiable GBDT or rules), confinement of agent actions (ch. 9), "human in the loop" for sensitive decisions;
5.  **Trace and respond**: logs of suspicious adversarial queries, post-mortems, adversarial tests in the CI — treat the attack as a reproducible bug;
6.  **Framework**: the AI Act (EU 2024/1689) classifies critical systems as high risk (ch. 10 of the Explainability-Security-Privacy module for the LLM variant); the NIST AI RMF provides the governance vocabulary.
:::

::: note
[Conclusion of the module]{.tag} The security of learning is not a property one adds at the end: it is an optimization constraint (min-max, ch. 4), a statistical guarantee (certification, ch. 5) and a process (protocols, monitoring, ch. 10) — on a common foundation: make the threat model explicit before anything else (ch. 1). The three "R"s to remember: *Realistic* (the adaptive attacker), *Rigorous* (proven attacks and guarantees), *Reproducible* (standardized evaluations).
:::

## Exercises / Labs {#ex}

1.  **FGSM/PGD on MNIST (ch. 2-3 — opening lab).** Train a small CNN; implement FGSM and PGD (thm. 3.2, def. 3.3); plot accuracy vs $\varepsilon$ for $K \in \{1, 7, 20, 50\}$ steps and 1/5/10 restarts; visualize the examples (MNIST grid at $\varepsilon \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.3\}$); measure white→black transfer to a second model (ch. 2).

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): clean CNN ≈ 99%; at $\varepsilon = 0.3$, FGSM drops accuracy below 10% (each pixel moves by a third of the dynamic range — thm. 3.2 in action); $K = 1$ (one-step PGD, null start) ≈ FGSM; the gain saturates quickly in $K$ (7 steps suffice), restarts add only a few tenths of a point at this budget — the real role of restarts appears on *defended* models (lab 2-3); transfer degrades but does not disappear (30-60% of the attack carries over to the target model): the "black box by secrecy of the weights" defense is futile. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
2.  **Adversarial training (ch. 4 — central lab).** PGD-AT (def. 4.1, 7 steps) on MNIST then CIFAR-10 at $\varepsilon = 8/255$; plot standard and robust accuracy per epoch on the same figure — *highlight the robust overfitting* (def. 4.3) and the trade-off of thm. 4.2; compare to TRADES (error decomposition); report the RobustBench grid (standard vs robust).

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): MNIST — standard accuracy \~98% (the trade-off of thm. 4.2 is small), robust at $\varepsilon = 0.3$ raised from \~0% to ≈ 90%; CIFAR-10 — standard \~95% → \~80% with AT, robust at 8/255 from \~0% to 45-50% (more with the augmentations of Rebuffi et al., 2021); robust overfitting is visible on CIFAR: test robustness peaks around the middle of training then decreases by several points while train robustness rises — early stopping and massive augmentation mitigate it (def. 4.3); TRADES gains a few robust points at equal standard by reading the boundary error. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
3.  **Standardized evaluation (ch. 3, 10).** Take the models from lab 2 and evaluate them with the AutoAttack library (APGD-CE, APGD-T, Square); compare to the "home-grown" PGD numbers; discuss the gap — then break a naive defense (e.g. re-training on FGSM adversaries only) with an *adaptive* attack (Athalye/Tramèr, ch. 4) and write the evaluation report in RobustBench format.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): on an *adversarially trained* model, AutoAttack and the home-grown PGD are close (the model has no masked gradient — a gap on the order of one point); on the naive defense (trained against FGSM only), the "home-grown" PGD overestimates robustness by tens of points and AutoAttack reveals the collapse: FGSM training *masks* the gradient (piecewise degraded, thm. 3.2 trapped) — the adaptive attack (reparameterization, smoothing) restores it; the honest report: standard accuracy, robust, budget $\varepsilon$, attack, restarts, cost — without these elements, no conclusion (def. 10.1). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
4.  **Certification (ch. 5).** Implement randomized smoothing: estimation of $g(x)$ and of the bounds $\underline{p_A}, \overline{p_B}$ (Clopper-Pearson, example 5.3) on MNIST at $\sigma \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1.0\}$; plot certified accuracy vs radius (thm. 5.2) and overlay it with the empirical accuracy ($L_2$ attacks); discuss the certification/empirical gap and the $\sigma$ accuracy/radius trade-off.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): at $\sigma = 0.25$, the smoothed classifier keeps a high clean accuracy but the certified radius quickly vanishes (R_max ≈ 0.3-0.4 on MNIST); at $\sigma = 1.0$, the certified radius reaches \~1 but the clean accuracy of the smoothed classifier drops — the certified accuracy vs radius curve is *below* the empirical curve everywhere, the gap measuring our ignorance (imperfect attacks from below, conservative certification from above); with $n = 10^4$ draws and $\alpha = 0.01$, Clopper-Pearson costs \~2 points of radius — the draw budget *is* a hyperparameter of the guarantee (example 5.3). [∎]{.qed}
    :::
5.  **Backdoor and detection (ch. 6).** Insert a BadNets trigger (3×3 patch) on 5% of MNIST; check clean accuracy vs trigger success rate; implement the Neural Cleanse reverse-engineering (def. 6.3: minimize $\\|\delta_c\\|_1$ per class, detect the MAD anomaly, reconstruct the trigger); repair by pruning then unlearning and measure the clean/trigger/repair triangle.

    ::: proof
    Guidance (expected results): with 5% of contaminated data, clean accuracy ≈ unchanged (98-99% — the attack is invisible to standard metrics, def. 6.1) and trigger success rate ≈ 99%; Neural Cleanse (def. 6.3) finds $\\|\delta_t\\|_1$ abnormally small *for the target class only* (MAD \> 3, the shortcut already exists); pruning the hyperactive neurons under the reconstructed trigger drops the trigger success but eats into clean accuracy from \~10% of removed neurons — hence the targeted unlearning (fine-tuning on reconstructed inputs) which restores the clean behavior without resurrecting the trigger; conclusion: repair is a trade-off, not a restoration. [∎]{.qed}
    :::
6.  **Poisoning and influence (ch. 7).** Label flipping on a tabular MLP: compare random flips vs "large margin" flips (prop. 7.2) at equal budget; compute the influence functions (Hessian-vector products) and show that the highest-influence flips explain the degradation; test the defenses: filtering by influence, truncated loss, regularization — conclude on the federated setting (referral to Emerging ML module ch. 4).
7.  **Extraction (ch. 8).** (i) Exact extraction of a logistic regression exposed by an API (prop. 8.2): verify the exact reconstruction, then with rounded probabilities (linear programming); (ii) distillation attack (Jagielski): measure accuracy *and* fidelity as a function of the query budget; (iii) discuss the defenses (rounding, top-1, quotas) and circumvent them.
8.  **Membership inference (ch. 8).** On a tabular MLP: shadow models + confidence attack (Shokri) then simplified LiRA (Carlini); plot ROC and TPR at FPR ∈ {0.1%, 1%, 10%}; retrain with DP-SGD (Opacus) at $\varepsilon \in \{1, 8\}$ and plot utility vs attack advantage — the trade-off curve of the Emerging ML module ch. 5, revisited from the attacker's side.
9.  **Final synthesis (ch. 9-10).** Write the complete threat analysis (def. 1.1) of a proposed real system (bank scoring, content filter, internal RAG agent): surface, capabilities, goals, applicable attacks chapter by chapter, defenses in depth (ch. 10) with their costs — a 10-minute defense with demonstrations drawn from the previous labs.
